summary: Defines an ALPN header field that lets an HTTP CONNECT request say which protocol will be spoken inside the tunnel once it is established. This helps proxies and servers know what to expect.

eli5.summary: Before a delivery truck goes through a tunnel, it posts a sign saying what language the passengers will speak.

questions: what is the alpn http header
how to signal the protocol in an http connect tunnel
how does a proxy know the protocol inside a connect tunnel
can a proxy trust the alpn header
how are alpn identifiers encoded in http
subtitle: A header that lets an HTTP CONNECT request announce which application protocol will run inside the tunnel.

tldr.problem: An HTTP CONNECT request asks a proxy to open a tunnel, but the proxy has no way to know what protocol the client plans to speak through it.
tldr.mechanism: The client adds an ALPN header field listing the Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation identifiers it intends to use inside the tunnel.
tldr.outcome: A proxy can reject or prioritize tunnels earlier and with better errors, but the header is optional, unprotected and can be falsified, so it is never enough to authorize a request.

today: RFC 7639 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2015, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why CONNECT Needs a Hint
sections.content:
The HTTP CONNECT method asks the recipient to set up a tunnel to an origin server and then forward packets in both directions until the tunnel is closed. Such tunnels are commonly used to create end-to-end virtual connections through one or more proxies.

RFC 7639 adds an ALPN header field to CONNECT requests. It names the protocol, or the set of protocols, that the client intends to use once the tunnel exists. It reuses the identifiers from Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation, defined in RFC 7301.

Proxies do not implement the tunneled protocol. They might still make policy decisions from the header value, for example choosing traffic prioritization.
sections.eli5: When you ask a gatekeeper to open a tunnel, you can also tell them what you will carry through it. That helps them decide how to treat you.

sections.title: Intent, Not Negotiation
sections.content:
The header carries an indication of client intent only. No negotiation takes place using it. In TLS, the final choice of application protocol is made by the server from the set of choices the client presents. Other substrates could negotiate the protocol differently.

When the tunnel will be secured with TLS, the header carries the same application protocol labels that will appear in the TLS handshake. If several protocols are possible, all of them are listed. An ALPN identifier here names an entire application protocol stack, not a single layer or component.

Where no negotiation is expected, such as protocols that do not use TLS, the header holds a single identifier for the intended protocol. If some other form of negotiation is possible, it holds the set of protocols that might be negotiated.
sections.eli5: The sign on the truck says what you hope to carry. The actual deal is still made with whoever is at the other end of the tunnel.

sections.title: Header Syntax and Encoding
sections.content:
Valid values come from the ALPN Protocol ID registry created by RFC 7301. The value is a comma-separated list of one or more protocol-id items, each a HTTP token.

ALPN protocol names are octet sequences with no format constraints, so octets that are not allowed in a token MUST be percent-encoded, as in RFC 3986. That includes the percent sign itself (hex 25). To give each name exactly one representation, octets that are valid token characters (other than %) MUST NOT be percent-encoded, and percent-encoding MUST use uppercase hex digits. Recipients can then match identifiers with simple string comparison.

The slash in http/1.1 is not a token character, which is why the example encodes it.

Example from the RFC: ALPN: h2, http%2F1.1 on a CONNECT www.example.com HTTP/1.1 request.
sections.eli5: Protocol names go on the sign as a list. Some characters can not be written on the sign directly, so they are swapped for a special code, always written the same way so everyone reads it alike.

sections.title: How Clients and Proxies Use It
sections.content:
For a tunnel carrying TLS, the header holds the same list of identifiers that will go in the TLS ClientHello message.

A proxy can use the value to reject CONNECT requests more cleanly and efficiently. Seeing the protocol at the HTTP layer lets it deny a request earlier and report better errors, such as a 403 status code. It can also use the value to change how it manages or prioritizes connections.

The alternative is to inspect packets to guess the protocol, which requires understanding every ALPN identifier. Protocols like TLS can hide the negotiated protocol, and negotiation details can change over time. For this reason proxies SHOULD NOT break a CONNECT tunnel solely because they fail to recognize the protocol.
sections.eli5: The guard can read the sign and say no right away, or move your truck to the right lane. Guessing from what is inside the truck is much harder.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The header is OPTIONAL. Clients and proxies may not support it, and if it is missing or ignored the proxy cannot learn the tunnel's purpose for authorization. That case looks the same as a client or proxy that simply lacks support.

There is no confidentiality protection for the header, so ALPN identifiers that might expose sensitive information SHOULD NOT be sent (see Section 5 of RFC 7301).

A client can falsify the value. If the tunnel data is encrypted, the proxy may be unable to check the claim, although it might use traffic analysis. A proxy therefore cannot rely on the header as a policy input in all cases. When CONNECT is used to reach a TURN server (RFC 5766), the warnings in Section 4.3.6 of RFC 7231 apply: proxies SHOULD restrict CONNECT to a limited set of known ports or a configurable whitelist of safe targets.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write anything on a sign, and the sign is visible to everyone. So the guard may use it as a hint but must not treat it as proof.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The RFC registers the header in the Permanent Message Header Field Names registry, following RFC 3864. The entry is: header field name ALPN, protocol http, status Standard, with the IETF (iesg@ietf.org) as change controller and Section 2 of this document as the reference.
sections.eli5: The new sign type was added to the official list of allowed signs, so everyone knows it exists.

data.title: CONNECT with an ALPN header
data.code:
CONNECT www.example.com HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
ALPN: h2, http%2F1.1
